Nineteen people were injured when an unidentified group (suspected CPN-Maoist Baidya cadres) hurled a petrol bomb into a moving bus at Basamadi VDC, Hetauda, Makwanpur District.
Keywords: CPN-Maoist, Maoist, Baidya, Basamadi, Makwanpur, Hetauda, bombing

Detail: The Supreme Court issued an interim order directing the poll-opposing 33-party alliance to call off their 10-day transport strike, ruling that while parties may boycott the election, they cannot infringe on the rights of others.
Six CPN-UML cadres were injured and 11 were unaccounted for after UCPN-M cadres (approximately 100) attacked the CPN-UML election publicity team at Purchaudi VDC, Baitadi District.
Keywords: UCPN-M, CPN-UML, Purchaudi, Baitadi, clash, elections

Detail: Raj Kumar Chettri, driver of a truck attacked with a petrol bomb in Bara District on November 14, succumbed to his injuries in Kathmandu — the first confirmed death directly attributed to the election disruption campaign.
Keywords: Bara, Kathmandu, killing, bombing, clash, elections

Detail: Five CPN-UML cadres were injured in a khukuri attack allegedly carried out by UCPN-M cadres in Rasuwa District.
A vehicle carrying water jars in Chitwan District was attacked with a petrol bomb by an unidentified group. The driver was injured.
Three NC cadres were injured after being attacked by CPN-UML cadres in Bhadaure VDC, Okhaldhunga District.
The second Constituent Assembly election was held. Over 70 percent of Nepal's 12 million voters participated, defying a boycott call and threats of violence by the 33-party alliance.
Three children were injured when a bomb exploded at Bhote Bahal in central Kathmandu while they were playing with it.
The Home Ministry reported that anti-poll groups placed explosive devices at 16 locations and suspicious objects at 32 locations across the country during the election period.
Police arrested 37 persons; 25 others were injured.

The National Human Rights Commission drew the Government's attention to the protection of the lives of the Adhikari couple and issued a statement urging Government compliance with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, calling for transitional justice-related matters to be addressed as a top priority.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: Rakesh Yadav, a transport worker injured when a petrol bomb was hurled at a bus in Bara District on November 14 during the bandh, died during treatment in Kathmandu — a second confirmed death from the election disruption campaign.
Netra Oli (22), a YCL cadre injured in a November 17 clash with CPN-UML cadres, died during treatment after being airlifted to Kathmandu.

UCPN-M sought "constitutional guarantee" of consensual politics, independent investigations into alleged election irregularities, and a renewed commitment to the 12-point agreement of 2005 that brokered the peace deal ending the decade-long Maoist conflict.

Police arrested Siyaram Kushwaha alias Firoj, the main accused in the murder of Kashi Tiwari in Chitwan District (shot dead on June 26, 2010 in Birgunj). Firoj was also a UCPN-M PR category candidate for the CA.

Supreme Court Rejects Blanket AmnestyThe Supreme Court rules that serious human rights violations, including torture, enforced disappearance, and extrajudicial killing, cannot be subject to blanket amnesty and directs the government to revise transitional justice legislation in line with victims' rights and international standards.

UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay issued a statement from Geneva welcoming the Supreme Court's January 2 decision against blanket amnesties for crimes committed during the 10-year conflict.
Secretary of CPN-Maoist Netra Bikram Chand warned that his party would be forced to wage another armed revolt if there were attempts to write the new constitution by sidelining the party.

CPN-Maoist-affiliated ANFA captured five bigha of land belonging to Devilal Dhakal in Nawalparasi District. A team led by the party's District Secretary hoisted a party flag on the land, claiming it would be distributed to landless farmers.
Two persons were injured when unidentified motorcyclists opened fire on them at Dhapakhel VDC, Lalitpur District. The injured were identified as Minkrishna Maharjan (42) and Milan Silwal (25).
The Government tabled six ordinances in the Legislature-Parliament, including one related to investigation into enforced disappearances and the formation of a TRC.
The Supreme Court issued summons to UCPN-M lawmaker Lalendra Kumar Mandal for his alleged involvement in a murder, responding to a writ petition seeking his arrest.
Organizations: Unified CPN-Maoist, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: The Okhaldhunga District Court sentenced five UCPN-M cadres to life imprisonment for the murder of CPN-UML leader Chabbi Lal Karki at the Tara Hotel in Okhaldhunga District three years earlier. Those convicted are Yadunath Ghimire, Tikaram Bhujel, Bimarsha Raj Ghimire, Nawaraj Basnet, and Dhan Bahadur Karki.
Keywords: UCPN-M, CPN-UML, The Okhaldhunga, Okhaldhunga, killing

Detail: Commemorating the 19th "People's War Day," both UCPN-M and CPN-Maoist expressed regret over their split.

UCPN-M leader Agni Sapkota urged the Government to form a TRC at the earliest to investigate all cases from the insurgency period, responding to Deputy PM Gautam's remarks about Government plans to punish those involved in conflict-era violations.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Unified CPN-Maoist

Detail: Three bigha and 13 kattha of land belonging to various religious trusts in Agyauli area, Nawalparasi District, were allegedly captured by CPN-Maoist, which arbitrarily distributed the land to "landless" people.
UCPN-M Chairman Dahal and CPN-Maoist Chairman Baidya signed a two-point deal opposing, among other things, the arrest of individuals alleged of rights violations during the armed conflict.

Nepal was scrutinised during the 110th session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on its "dismal" rights record, including the inordinate delay in forming transitional justice mechanisms to redress the plight of those directly affected by the decade-long Maoist conflict.

The Government assured the Legislature-Parliament that it would bring bills on the TRC and Commission on Enforced Disappearances to address cases of human rights violations that occurred during the Maoist insurgency.

The National Victims Alliance expressed strong reservations against the involvement of Dinesh Tripathi and Chunda Bahadur Shrestha in the 11-member taskforce formed by the Government to prepare draft bills related to the TRC and Disappearance Commission, citing concerns about victims' interests.

An expert committee formed to finalise bills on the TRC and Commission on Enforced Disappearances began consultations with stakeholders, and announced it would seek input from political party representatives and victims.

CPN-Maoist Chairman Mohan Baidya challenged the authorities to arrest him rather than arresting party cadres over conflict-era cases, saying: "Pushpa Kamal Dahal, Baburam Bhattarai and I led the people's war. If the Government is bold enough then it should arrest me first."

UCPN-M leader Baburam Bhattarai challenged the authorities to initiate legal action against him for conflict-era murders and rights abuses, saying that as head of the then Maoist People's Government he would take full responsibility "for all the acts committed during that period."

The Supreme Court ruled that conflict-era cases can be tried under existing laws, at a time when both Maoist parties were continuously pressuring political leadership not to take up insurgency-era cases until the TRC and Disappearance Commission were formed.
Keywords: Maoist, TRC, Supreme Court, transitional justice
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: A 13-member Task Force formed by the Government to prepare new draft bills for a TRC and a Commission on Enforced Disappearance submitted three draft bills for both transitional mechanisms.

UCPN-M leaders met Prime Minister Sushil Koirala to express concern about what they called the "unilateral" reform of the bills on TRC and Commission on Enforced Disappearances, and called for downsizing the "negative list" for granting amnesty.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Unified CPN-Maoist

Detail: Leaders of the ruling coalition partners NC and CPN-UML stressed the need to form the TRC in a way that would not grant general amnesty to perpetrators without victim consent.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CPN-UML, Nepali Congress

Detail: The Government tabled a revised bill on TRC and Commission on Enforced Disappearances with special focus on reconciliation, proposing a judicial commission with powers akin to a court for a two-year term, and giving authority to the commission to proceed with reconciliation if either a perpetrator or victim files for it.
Legal experts warned that the Government's TRC and CED bill was against national and international laws, and that it could face a Supreme Court challenge.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: NC, CPN-UML, and UCPN-M reached an understanding to stand united in Parliament to endorse the bill on TRC and CED.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Unified CPN-Maoist, CPN-UML, Nepali Congress

Detail: The Government filed a charge-sheet against 13 Maoist cadres at Chitwan District Court for the killing of Krishna Prasad Adhikari, a resident of Gorkha District, on June 6, 2004.

UCPN-M Chairman Dahal warned that the nation could face serious confrontation if the Government failed to commit to the TRC. The following day the party boycotted a scheduled three-party meeting in protest at the filing of cases and warned of further protests, threatening not to show up in any political meeting unless the cases were withdrawn.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Unified CPN-Maoist

Detail: Conflict victims, at a program in Kathmandu, raised a common concern that the TRC bill had to be amended before endorsement by Parliament.
UCPN-M obstructed Parliament proceedings, protesting the Government's filing of a charge-sheet against 13 Maoist cadres accused of murdering Krishna Prasad Adhikari.
Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the International Commission of Jurists expressed grave concern over the amnesty provision contained in the TRC bill before Nepal's Parliament.
Organizations: Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, International Commission of Jurists, Truth and Reconciliation Commission

Detail: Following two consecutive days of disruption by UCPN-M, Minister for Law Narhari Acharya tabled the bills on TRC and Commission on Enforced Disappearances in the Legislature-Parliament.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Unified CPN-Maoist

Detail: Conflict victims and lawmakers from various parties voiced concern during Parliament deliberations on the TRC and CED bills, with victims calling for the bills to be amended before endorsement.

The Parliament passed the bills on the formation of the TRC and the Commission on Enforced Disappearances (CED) with amendment. The term "disappearance" was replaced with "enforced disappearance" following the amendment.
Twelve organisations of conflict victims issued a joint press statement demanding that the TRC and CED bill be amended and made "victims-friendly."
TRC Act EnactedParliament adopts the Commission on Investigation of Disappeared Persons, Truth and Reconciliation Act.
An IED was recovered from the premises of Shree Janakalyan Higher Secondary School in Purandhara VDC, western Dang District — targeting civilian educational infrastructure.
PM Sushil Koirala defended the Transitional Justice Bill passed on April 25, claiming it aimed at national unity and reconciliation and had not deviated from international standards.

President Ram Baran Yadav approved the Transitional Justice Bill, enacting the Commission on Investigation of Disappeared Persons, Truth and Reconciliation Act (TRC Act), establishing the TRC and CEIDP. Despite previous Supreme Court orders, the Act retained amnesty provisions. Conflict victims, civil society, and the international community issued statements of rejection.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: The Government acknowledged a significant drafting error: the TRC Act stated that a former Chief Justice must chair the recommendation committee for both commissions, contradicting Article 106(2) of the Interim Constitution, which prohibits such appointments.

Former CPN-Maoist cadre Pushkar Gautam, convicted by the Okhaldhunga District Court for killing Ujjan Kumar Shrestha of Tarkerabari on June 24, 1998, was arrested in Okhaldhunga District after two years as a fugitive and sent to serve his life sentence.
Police recovered 323 bomb-making socket components from an individual in Jajarkot District.
Police recovered nine kilograms of explosive materials from a forest in Jajarkot District.

Suman Adhikari and 234 others — victims from both the rebel and state sides — filed a writ petition at the Supreme Court against the TRC Act, arguing that sections 13, 22, 24, 25, 26, and 29 of the Act were incompatible with the Interim Constitution, international human rights and humanitarian laws, principles of transitional justice, and prior Supreme Court orders.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: A suspected pressure cooker bomb (later found to be a hoax) was planted at Gate No. 3 of the CA building at New Baneshwor, Kathmandu. Leaflets printed in the name of "Dalit Mukti Force" were recovered nearby.

The Supreme Court set July 10 as the date to begin hearing the petition challenging the TRC Act, filed by 234 conflict victims who alleged the Act's amnesty and reconciliation provisions were inconsistent with the Court's earlier orders.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: The Government began the process of forming commissions for the TRC and CED. The Cabinet formed a committee headed by former Chief Justice Ombhakta Shrestha to recommend names for both commissions.
UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon stressed the need for a credible TRC in line with international standards during a meeting with Prime Minister Sushil Koirala in New York.
UNOHCHR urged the Government to amend the TRC and CED Act to make it fully consistent with Nepal's obligations under international law.

A sub-committee of the CA's Political Dialogue and Consensus Committee held talks with 45 parties outside the CA — including armed outfits operational in Eastern Hills and Mid-Tarai — on July 7 and 8, as part of efforts to bring armed groups into the mainstream.

The Government maintained in a written reply to the Supreme Court that perpetrators of serious crimes during the conflict cannot be granted amnesty unless the victim is convinced by the perpetrator's apology. The Chief Secretary argued the TRC Act did not envision blanket amnesty for serious crimes.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Police arrested two former CPN-Maoist combatants, Roka Magar (25) and Ujir Bahadur Magar (38), at Dharapani Police Post in Manang District after they attempted to attack on-duty Police personnel.
Police recovered one AK-47 rifle, 32 rounds of ammunition, one Chinese pistol, and a home-made pistol from their possession.

Five armed outfits active in the Tarai region pledged to give up their armed struggle to join the constitution-making process and peaceful politics, in meetings held in Janakpur, Dhanusa District, initiated by the CA's Political Dialogue and Consensus Committee.

Minister of Law Narhari Acharya assured the Legislature-Parliament that the Government was committed to implementing agreements on relief packages for conflict victims, addressing UCPN-M's demand that the Government commit in the budget to carrying out relief programmes for conflict victims.
Police arrested nine CPN-Maoist cadres in Chitwan District (seven from Ratnanagar and two from Narayangadh) for enforcing a bandh on August 25.
The Conflict Victims' Common Platform (CVCP) was formally established to unite conflict victims and their organisations and advocate for a victim-centred transitional justice process.

The Recommendation Committee — responsible for nominating the chairperson and members of the TRC and the CED — endorsed its working procedure and decided to invite applications from eligible candidates for the posts, giving new impetus to the transitional justice process.

Nanda Prasad Adhikary, father of Krishna Prasad Adhikary (killed by Maoists in 2004), died at Bir Hospital on the 333rd day of his hunger strike demanding justice, aged 52. His body remained uncremated in the mortuary of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, Kathmandu. His wife, Ganga Maya Adhikary, continued the hunger strike.

Human Rights Watch published Silenced and Forgotten: Survivors of Nepal’s Conflict-Era Sexual Violence, documenting rape and other sexual violence by both state security forces and Maoist combatants, survivors’ exclusion from the Interim Relief Program, barriers including Nepal’s short rape-reporting limitation period, and calling for justice and reparations.
Keywords: Human Rights Watch, Silenced and Forgotten, conflict-related sexual violence, Interim Relief Program, impunity, Advocacy Forum
Organizations: Human Rights Watch; Advocacy Forum (field partnership noted in report)

Detail: The NHRC appointed its member Sudip Pathak as its representative on the recommendation committee for the formation of TRC and CED, completing the five-member committee and enabling it to start work after approximately four months of delay due to vacancies. As per the TRC and CED Act, the NHRC chairperson or a person designated by them must serve as a member of the committee.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal, Truth and Reconciliation Commission

Detail: Victims of the decade-long armed conflict submitted a memorandum to the Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction, demanding amendment of the TRC and CED Act and asking the recommendation committee to halt its work while related cases remained sub judice at the Supreme Court. The victims demanded the Act be amended in line with previous Supreme Court rulings.
Organizations: Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction, Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Speaking at a consultation programme organised by the NHRC, Commission Chairman Anup Raj Sharma warned the NHRC could withdraw its representative from the TRC and CEIDP if the transitional justice mechanisms provided amnesty to persons involved in heinous human rights violations. Sharma said serious violations, even from the conflict period, should be dealt with by regular courts.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal, Truth and Reconciliation Commission

Detail: CPN-Maoist faction Secretary Netra Bikram Chand threatened to launch another round of armed insurgency should his group be excluded from the country's political process. Chand said they would "go for revolution" if mainstream parties continued to bypass them, and announced the party needed its own army to fight for the people's welfare.

The Mohan Baidya-led CPN-Maoist split as a faction led by Secretary Netra Bikram Chand formally announced its separation, submitting a letter to the CPN-Maoist central committee. The Chand-led faction cited irreconcilable differences over political strategy and leadership.
The CPDCC decided to ask the Government to expedite the process of forming the TRC and Disappearance Commission, to provide transitional justice to conflict victims.

Netra Bikram Chand formally announced the formation of a new Communist Party of Nepal-Maoist (CPN-M), to hold its first national convention January 7–10, 2015. Chand stated the party had no plans to launch an armed revolt but was "ready to retaliate if the government tries to suppress their struggle."

Various conflict victim organisations accused the Government of ignoring those rendered disabled by the decade-long conflict and warned of protest if their demands were not addressed. They submitted a memorandum to the Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction calling for data collection on conflict-disabled persons.

The Dailekh District Court convicted five persons for the 2004 murder of journalist Dekendra Thapa, a correspondent for state-owned Radio Nepal who was abducted on June 26, 2004, and killed by Maoist cadres on August 11, 2004. Those convicted: Jaya Bahadur Sahi, Hira Lal Pun, Nirak KC, Bir Bahadur Gharti, and Laxmiram Gharti.
Keywords: Maoist, The Dailekh, Dailekh, abduction, killing, press

Detail: Top leaders of NC, CPN-UML, and UCPN-M expressed their commitment to provide all necessary support to the recommendation committee for the formation of the TRC and the CED.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Unified CPN-Maoist, CPN-UML, Nepali Congress

Detail: PM Sushil Koirala acknowledged the need to uphold human rights but remained non-committal on conflict victims' issues at an event marking Human Rights Day.

A sub-committee of the CA's Political Dialogue and Consensus Committee reached an understanding with Terai Madhes Tigers, an armed outfit active in the central southern plains of Nepal, in talks held in Bhairahawa, Rupandehi. The outfit's leader Jai Prakash Yadav signed a four-point agreement with the team.

The Nepal Bar Association (NBA) released a report concluding that the TRC and Commission for Investigation of Disappeared Persons Formation Act 2014 needed amendment. An expert committee, led by former Justice Pawan Kumar Ojha, found the Act was not fully in line with international standards or previous Supreme Court verdicts on transitional justice.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Netra Bikram Chand announced at a cadres' meet in Bharatpur, Chitwan, that his faction was launching "a new revolution," without specifying its form, as he was unable to see any real change after the country's major political transformations.

were injured in clashes between UCPN-M-led alliance activists and police across the country. In Kavre, 12 protesters and 5 police were injured. In Chitwan, 7 people including 2 police were injured at Bharatpur. In Rupandehi, 9 protesters were injured in Bhairahawa. In Rautahat, 6 protesters and 2 police were injured in Gaur. In Sindhuli, DSP Shyam Kumar Mahato was injured.
Keywords: UCPN-M, police, Kavre, Chitwan, Rupandehi, Rautahat, clash, protest

Detail: including 8 security force personnel were injured on the first day of a three-day general strike called by the UCPN-M-led 30-party alliance. In Kavre, 8 police and 12 strike enforcers were injured in clashes during a torch rally. In Bhairahawa, strike supporters set ablaze a motorcycle.
At least 19 vehicles were vandalised and 4 vehicles set ablaze.
people including security force personnel were injured in clashes in Dhanusha, Bara, and Rupandehi Districts as Madhesi Morcha enforced a strike in the plains. In Janakpur, 15 people were injured.
Keywords: Dhanusha, Bara, Rupandehi, Janakpur, clash, protest

Detail: Police used tear gas and batons to disperse protesters. In Bara, some 30 people were injured. The NHRC urged the government to show restraint and avoid use of excessive force.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: cadres and 12 police were injured as clashes erupted during President Bidhya Devi Bhandari's visit to the Janaki temple in Janakpur, Dhanusha District.
An unidentified assailant hurled a petrol bomb at Dish Home Control Unit offices in Lalitpur.

Concerns Raised Regarding Independence and Legal FrameworkVictims' groups and human rights organizations raise concerns that unresolved legal deficiencies and amnesty-related provisions could undermine the credibility of the commissions.

TRC and CIEDP Established and Concerns Raised Regarding Independence and Legal FrameworkNepal appoints commissioners to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons.

A special constitutional bench of Nepal’s Supreme Court (Justices Kalyan Shrestha, Baidhya Nath Upadhyay, Cholendra Shumsher JB Rana), deciding a writ filed by more than 200 conflict victims (Suman Adhikari et al. v. Prime Minister, 070-WS-0050), struck down TRC Act amnesty provisions (notably §26(2)) and held that reconciliation requires victim consent and that only courts — not the commissions — determine criminal liability for serious conflict-era violations. The Court ordered amendments consistent with the Interim Constitution, treaty obligations, and its earlier 2 January 2014 ordinance ruling.
Keywords: Supreme Court, TRC Act, amnesty, Suman Adhikari, conflict victims, CIEDP, transitional justice
Organizations: Supreme Court of Nepal; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons

Detail: Gorkha EarthquakeNational attention and resources shift substantially away from transitional justice implementation.

In Tikapur, Kailali, during Tharu protests against proposed federal boundaries ahead of the new constitution, protesters attacked security personnel; eight Nepal Police / Armed Police Force officers (including SSP Laxman Neupane) were killed, and an infant child of an APF officer also died. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty later documented both the police killings and subsequent alleged arbitrary detention, torture, and coerced confessions of Tharu detainees. The incident marked a sharp escalation of Terai violence before constitution promulgation and the Madhes blockade.
Keywords: Tikapur, Kailali, Tharu, Tharuhat, Madhes, constitution protests, police killings, SSP Laxman Neupane
Organizations: Nepal Police; Armed Police Force; Tharuhat Struggle Committee (protesters)

Detail: First meeting between TRC commission officials and conflict victim networks held at Naya Baneshwar Alpha Beta Hall, Kathmandu. Commission officials attended the venue victims had specified (Annapurna Hotel), but the victims who were invited did not attend. Victims also did not go to the commission office. The disconnect illustrated the early breakdown of trust between victims and the commissions.
Constitution of Nepal Promulgated

Following promulgation of the Constitution of Nepal on 20 September 2015, Madhesi and allied protesters blocked major India–Nepal border crossing points (notably around Birgunj), disrupting fuel and essential supplies. Nepal’s government later characterised the crisis as an Indian “blockade”; India attributed obstructions to insecurity and protests on the Nepal side. The supply crisis continued for months into early 2016.
Keywords: Madhes, constitution 2015, border blockade, Birgunj, UDMF, India-Nepal, fuel crisis, Tharu
Organizations: United Democratic Madhesi Front (UDMF); Government of Nepal

Detail: Parliament elected CPN-UML leader K.P. Sharma Oli as Nepal’s 38th prime minister (338–249 over incumbent Sushil Koirala), the first PM chosen after the 20 September 2015 Constitution. He was sworn in on 12 October amid continuing Madhesi protests and the border supply crisis.
Keywords: KP Sharma Oli, Prime Minister, CPN-UML, Constitution 2015, Madhes crisis

Detail: Human Rights Watch published “Like We Are Not Nepali”: Protest and Police Crackdown in the Terai Region of Nepal, documenting unlawful use of lethal force by security forces against Madhesi and Tharu protesters after mid-August 2015, the 24 August Tikapur police killings, and broader patterns of excessive force during the constitution protests and ensuing unrest.
Keywords: Human Rights Watch, Terai, Madhes, Tharu, police crackdown, constitution protests, Tikapur

Detail: The TRC began consultations with conflict victims, civil society representatives, and local authorities in Rukum District.
Supreme Court Reaffirms Limits on AmnestyThe Court reiterates that serious human rights violations cannot be subject to blanket amnesty.
The TRC and CIEDP informed Parliament that political disagreements were delaying approval of regulations necessary for their work.
TRC Chairperson Surya Kiran Gurung warned that failure to address conflict-era violations could result in increased international involvement in Nepal’s transitional justice process.
Conflict victims met with the National Human Rights Commission to discuss concerns regarding justice and accountability.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: Nepal’s Parliament passed the First Amendment to the Constitution of Nepal 2015, amending provisions on proportional inclusion and constituency delimitation (commonly cited Articles 42, 84, 286) in response to Madhesi demands after months of Terai protests and the India-border supply blockade. President Bidhya Devi Bhandari authenticated the amendment bill on 28 February 2016.
Keywords: First Amendment, Constitution 2015, Madhes, proportional representation, electoral constituencies
Organizations: Parliament of Nepal; Office of the President

Detail: After about 135 days, the United Democratic Madhesi Front (UDMF) and allied Madhesi parties formally called off the India–Nepal border blockade / protest programme that began after the September 2015 constitution promulgation, while stating that core demands remained unmet. Fuel and essential-goods shortages that had compounded post-earthquake hardship eased thereafter.
Keywords: Madhes blockade, UDMF, India–Nepal border, Constitution 2015, Terai

Detail: The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights stated that it could not support the TRC and CIEDP unless Nepal amended the TRC Act to comply with international law.
The TRC and CIEDP announced plans to begin collecting complaints and conduct detailed investigations into conflict-era violations.

Police injured five protesters and detained several conflict victims, including Charan Prasai, Ram Bhandari, Kamala Rai, and Lenin Bista, during a demonstration in Kathmandu marking the International Day for the Right to Truth.
The Conflict Victims Common Platform submitted a memorandum to the government demanding legal and structural reforms to the TRC and CIEDP.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP, Conflict Victims Common Platform

Detail: 11 August 2016 – The TRC conducted a nationwide complaint registration campaign and collected 58,052 complaints relating to conflict-era violations.
The CIEDP began receiving complaints from families of persons subjected to enforced disappearance during the armed conflict.

The CPN-UML and UCPN (Maoist) signed a nine-point political agreement that included commitments to withdraw conflict-era court cases and facilitate amnesty provisions. Victims, civil society organizations, and international actors strongly opposed the agreement, arguing it violated Supreme Court rulings and Nepal’s international obligations.
The Conflict Victims Common Platform stated that the nine-point agreement undermined the transitional justice process and victims’ rights.
Lawyers filed a writ petition before the Supreme Court challenging provisions of the nine-point agreement related to withdrawal of conflict-era cases.

The TRC began preliminary investigations into complaints received from conflict victims. Victims of the Madi bus bombing, in which civilians were killed in 2005, submitted complaints to the commission.

Diplomatic missions from Australia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union urged Nepal to uphold its national and international human rights obligations while addressing conflict-era violations.
Families of 17 labourers killed in a military operation in 2002 filed complaints with the TRC against former Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba and former Nepal Army chief Rookmangud Katawal.
Keywords: Nepal Army, TRC, killing, transitional justice
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Nepal Army

Detail: TRC Chairperson Surya Kiran Gurung stated that there should be no amnesty for serious conflict-era crimes.

Krishna K.C. filed a complaint with the TRC against former King Gyanendra Shah and five former prime ministers, alleging responsibility for his arbitrary detention by the Nepal Army during the conflict.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Nepal Army

Detail: The TRC extended the complaint registration deadline after requests from victims. Conflict victims in Kanchanpur also raised concerns about confidentiality and protection of complainants.
Families of conflict victims filed a complaint against former Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba regarding alleged serious human rights violations during the conflict.
A complaint was filed against former Prime Minister Baburam Bhattarai alleging responsibility for conflict-era human rights violations.
The TRC finalized investigation procedures intended to align with international standards and facilitate investigations into registered complaints.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the enforced disappearance of Milan Nepali, a Maoist-affiliated journalist arrested by police in 1999 and never seen again, and ruled that Nepal had violated his rights to life, liberty, freedom from torture, and legal recognition.
The TRC extended the deadline for complaint registration until 10 August to allow more victims to participate.
Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal publicly advocated a “forgive and forget” approach to conflict-era cases, prompting concern among victims and human rights advocates.
Prime Minister Dahal assured the TRC that the government was not pursuing blanket amnesty for conflict-era violations. Commissioners reiterated the need to amend the TRC Act and criminalize torture.
CIEDP officials warned that limited resources and the complexity of disappearance investigations would significantly delay efforts to determine the fate of missing persons.
Conflict victims threatened legal action against the TRC over guidelines that could allow investigations into conflict-era complaints to be suspended.
Parliament’s Social Justice and Human Rights Committee instructed the government to amend the TRC and CIEDP Act in accordance with Supreme Court rulings and international standards.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, Supreme Court, transitional justice
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: The Conflict Victims’ National Society objected to TRC procedures that it argued could enable amnesty for perpetrators of serious crimes.
The International Committee of the Red Cross and Nepal Red Cross Society published an updated list identifying 1,334 disappeared persons from the conflict period.
The CIEDP formally requested urgent amendment of the TRC Act, stating that existing legislation was insufficient to effectively investigate enforced disappearances.
Conflict victims organized sit-ins and demonstrations in Kathmandu demanding amendment of the TRC Act and stronger protections for victims' rights.

The government formed a high-level probe commission chaired by former Supreme Court Justice Girish Chandra Lal to investigate killings, excessive force, and other abuses during the 2015 Terai/Madhes constitution protests. The commission later received thousands of complaints and submitted its report on 16 December 2017; the report has remained largely unpublished despite court pressure (publication fight is later — not collapsed into this row).
Keywords: Lal Commission, Girish Chandra Lal, Madhes, Terai protests 2015, inquiry

Detail: Human rights organizations called for the removal of statutes of limitations for torture committed during the armed conflict.
The TRC reported beginning preliminary investigations into more than 25,000 complaints, while the CIEDP was reviewing approximately 1,200 disappearance cases.
Conflict victims expressed concern over proposed amendments that would remove crimes against humanity from the category of serious crimes.
The Supreme Court issued an interim order preventing the TRC from implementing guidelines that allowed complaints to be put on hold without investigation.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: The TRC proposed 18 forms of reparation for victims and families affected by conflict-era killings, including education support, vocational training, housing assistance, and psychosocial counseling.

Police arrested 169 former Maoist child soldiers who were protesting in Kathmandu demanding recognition and justice. The group had been disqualified from integration into the national army after the conflict.
Keywords: police, Maoist, Kathmandu, demobilisation, children, protest

Detail: The TRC reported that delays in legal reform, government approvals, and funding had prevented substantive investigations despite receiving more than 57,000 complaints.
On the tenth anniversary of the Comprehensive Peace Accord, victims and observers noted that key commitments regarding truth, disappearances, and accountability remained unfulfilled.
The heads of the TRC and CIEDP publicly criticized the government for failing to provide adequate legal, financial, and institutional support.
The government failed to table amendments to the TRC Act in Parliament, delaying further progress in transitional justice.
The Conflict Victims’ National Society submitted a memorandum to Sher Bahadur Deuba, urging political leaders to prioritize transitional justice.
Internal disagreements within the TRC delayed adoption of proposed reparation guidelines for conflict victims.
Prime Minister Pushpa Kamal Dahal called on Maoist leaders and supporters to unite in protecting the political gains achieved through the armed conflict.

TRC and CIEDP Receive Tens of Thousands of ComplaintsThe commissions register large numbers of conflict-era complaints but make little progress toward investigation, truth recovery, prosecution recommendations, or reparations.
The Supreme Court ordered the development of legislation enabling the transfer of property belonging to forcibly disappeared persons to their families.
The TRC expanded its operations by establishing offices in all seven provinces to facilitate investigations and victim engagement.
Human Rights Watch reported that Nepal had failed to ensure accountability for conflict-era human rights violations and warned that justice efforts remained stalled.
The TRC and CIEDP requested a one-year extension of their mandates, citing the need to continue investigations into more than 58,000 conflict-related complaints.
The Supreme Court struck down TRC guidelines that could have allowed thousands of conflict-era cases to be suspended without investigation.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: The TRC formally requested a one-year extension of its mandate from the government.
The Government extended the mandates of the TRC and CIEDP by one year after both commissions failed to complete their work within the original timeframe.
Conflict victims, civil society organizations, and international actors renewed calls to amend the TRC Act to bring it into line with national and international legal standards.
The International Commission of Jurists stated that extending the commissions’ mandates without amending the law would not advance justice or accountability.
The Conflict Victims National Society observed a “Black Day” in Kathmandu, demanding justice for conflict-era violations.
The TRC and CIEDP announced plans to reopen complaint registration for conflict victims.
UN Resident Coordinator Valerie Julliand urged Nepal to ensure that the work of the TRC and CIEDP complied with international standards.
A draft bill proposing the creation of a Transitional Justice Special Court was reviewed by the Supreme Court.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the enforced disappearance, torture, and death of Padman Narayan Nakarmi, a civilian ironmonger arrested by the Royal Nepal Army in 2003. The Committee found violations of his rights to life, liberty, freedom from torture, and legal recognition.
Conflict victims demanded the resignation of TRC officials, accusing the commission of delaying investigations into conflict-era violations.
A government task force verified an additional 3,830 conflict victims for inclusion in state support and recognition mechanisms.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the rape and torture of Purna Maya, a civilian woman assaulted by Royal Nepal Army personnel in Dailekh in 2004. The ruling marked the first international decision on a conflict-related sexual violence case from Nepal.
The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the enforced disappearance of Rajendra Prasad Dhakal, a lawyer and human rights defender arrested by police in 1999 and never seen again.
A government task force began fieldwork to collect information on conflict-affected individuals and families.
The TRC adopted a work plan committing to begin preliminary investigations into conflict-era complaints.
The CIEDP warned that the absence of legislation criminalizing torture continued to hinder investigations.

The Kavre District Court sentenced three Nepal Army officers to life imprisonment for the murder of Maina Sunuwar (15), a schoolgirl tortured and killed in military custody in 2004. This was the first conviction of Nepal Army personnel for a conflict-era crime.
Keywords: Nepal Army, The Kavre, Kavre, killing

Detail: The United Nations welcomed the conviction in the Maina Sunuwar case and called for the sentences to be implemented without delay.
A TRC commissioner called for urgent action to address delays in the commission’s work.
The TRC began investigations into more than 10,000 complaints in Province 6 and expanded provincial operations to process conflict-era cases.
The chairs of the TRC and CIEDP informed Parliament that transitional justice remained stalled due to delays in amending the governing legislation.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the enforced disappearance of Danda Pani Neupane, a Maoist party member arrested in 1999 and never seen again, and for violating his rights to life, liberty, and freedom from torture.
The TRC reported receiving 61,615 complaints, while the CIEDP reported 2,506 complaints related to enforced disappearances.
Families of disappeared persons expressed frustration over slow progress in investigations during an event marking the International Day of the Disappeared.

The National Human Rights Commission noted that the fate of many disappeared persons remained unknown more than a decade after the Comprehensive Peace Accord and called for impartial investigations and reparations.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: Police arrested Bal Krishna Dhungel, a Maoist leader convicted in the 1998 killing of Ujjan Kumar Shrestha, prompting criticism from the CPN (Maoist Centre).
The International Commission of Jurists reported that impunity for serious human rights violations remained a major obstacle to democracy and the rule of law in Nepal.
Pushpa Kamal Dahal publicly described the Bandarmudhe bus bombing of 2005, in which 38 civilians were killed, as one of the Maoists’ greatest mistakes during the armed conflict.
The first phase of Nepal’s federal parliamentary and provincial elections was held, marking the country's first federal elections under the new constitutional framework.
Pushpa Kamal Dahal signed an agreement with families of victims of the Bandarmudhe massacre, amid criticism that transitional justice mechanisms had failed to deliver accountability.
Conflict victims criticized the TRC for failing to follow due process in its investigations and for not adequately addressing their concerns.
Nepal completed the second phase of federal parliamentary and provincial elections.
The Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction accelerated efforts to amend the law governing the TRC and CIEDP.
Organizations: Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction, Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP

Detail: The Conflict Victims Common Platform accused the CIEDP of transferring disappearance cases to the TRC without conducting proper investigations, raising concerns among families of the disappeared.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP, Conflict Victims Common Platform

Detail: First Commissioners Leave Office Without Completing Core MandateThe terms of the first commissioners expire without completing investigations, truth-seeking, or recommendations for accountability, reinforcing concerns regarding the effectiveness of the process.
The Conflict Victim Common Platform published Living Memories of War – Part One, a collection of fourteen testimonies by conflict-affected persons with disabilities.

The Government of Nepal extended the mandates of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) and the Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons (CIEDP) by one year without amending the TRC Act.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP, Government of Nepal

Detail: The Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction was dissolved.

The TRC and CIEDP received a third mandate extension. Conflict victims and international actors renewed calls for amendment of the TRC Act to align it with victims’ rights and international standards.
Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli stated publicly that there should be no general amnesty for serious conflict-era crimes.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the enforced disappearance and torture of Himal Sharma, arrested by security forces in Kathmandu in October 2003 and held incommunicado for more than two years at Bhairabnath Battalion barracks.
The Conflict Victims’ Common Platform submitted a letter to the Ministry of Law demanding meaningful consultation with victims in the amendment of the TRC Act.

The Government introduced a bill to amend the TRC Act. Victims’ groups and civil society criticized the process for inadequate consultation and proposed provisions allowing only symbolic punishment for serious violations. CVCP preliminary comments followed on 17 July 2018 (already in mastersheet) and Amnesty/ICJ/TRIAL International preliminary comments on 20 July 2018 (appended as a separate event).
Civil society organizations and conflict victims conducted consultations in 13 districts on proposed amendments to the TRC Act.
The National Human Rights Commission called on the Government to protect the life of Gangamaya Adhikari, who continued her long campaign for justice for the killing of her son during the conflict.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: The National Human Rights Commission submitted recommendations to the Government for its report to the UN Committee Against Torture.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: The Conflict Victims’ Common Platform released preliminary comments on the Government’s proposed amendments to the TRC Act.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the enforced disappearance and killing of Hari Prasad Bolakhe, a Christian pastor arrested by security forces in Kavre District. His remains were exhumed from a forest in 2006.

Amnesty International, the International Commission of Jurists, and TRIAL International published Preliminary Comments on Draft Bill to Amend the Act on Commission on Investigation of Disappeared Persons, Truth and Reconciliation, 2018 (ASA 31/8817/2018), criticising inadequate consultation with victims, weakening of crimes-against-humanity language, and sentencing/accountability gaps relative to Supreme Court jurisprudence and international standards — days after CVCP’s 17 July minimum demands (already in mastersheet).
Keywords: Amnesty International, ICJ, TRIAL International, TRC Act amendment, transitional justice, consultation
Organizations: Amnesty International; International Commission of Jurists; TRIAL International

Detail: Nirmala Pant, a 13-year-old girl from Kanchanpur District, went missing while visiting a friend’s home.
The body of Nirmala Pant, 13, was found in Kanchanpur District. The case sparked nationwide demands for justice and accountability.

The Conflict Victims’ Common Platform published a White Paper on transitional justice, prompting debate among victims’ groups and civil society. The same National Conference of Conflict Victims on Transitional Justice (Kamaladi, Kathmandu, 20–21 Nov 2018) adopted the 23-point Conflict Victims’ Charter (Dwanda Piditko Badapatra), rejecting status-quo TRC/CIEDP practice and demanding victim-consented law reform and a high-level transitional justice mechanism.
Keywords: Conflict Victims’ Charter, Dwanda Piditko Badapatra, National Conference

Detail: A case was filed against police officials in connection with the investigation into the rape and killing of Nirmala Pant.
Formation of the Conflict Victims National Alliance (CVNA) — Declaration of the Alliance.

The TRC and CEIDP, having collected over 60,000 cases but completed no investigations in four years, had their mandates extended by six months ahead of their expiry on 9 February. Appointed commissioners' terms were set to expire on 15 April.
Term of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Commission for Investigation of Disappeared Persons expired.
Civil society, conflict victims, and the international community again demand amendment of the Act. Position that only after amendment will the commission be established is made public.

First-ever consultative discussion with political party leaders, retired army generals, the international community, and victims: "What can be done in transitional justice?" — organized by the US Embassy.

On 18 March 2019 the UN Human Rights Committee adopted Views in Fulmati Nyaya v. Nepal (communication filed 20 June 2014 via TRIAL International), finding Nepal responsible for conflict-related sexual violence and related violations against the indigenous Tharu girl known by the pseudonym Fulmati Nyaya — the first conflict-related sexual violence Views against Nepal under the Optional Protocol. (Underlying April 2002 incident recorded separately.)
The Council of Ministers decides to form a Recommendation Committee to recommend new members of the Commissions.

The Government nominates a 5-member recommendation committee under the chairmanship of a former Chief Justice, Mr. Om Prakash Mishra, to recommend names of new commissioners under the existing Commission of Inquiry on Disappearances, Truth and Reconciliation Act 2014
A recommendation committee led by former Chief Justice Om Prakash Mishra was formed to select candidates for the TRC and CEIDP.

UN experts sent a joint letter to Foreign Affairs Minister Pradeep Kumar Gyawali, expressing concern over the lack of impartiality and transparency in the commission appointment process and calling on the government to amend the TRC Act in consultation with victims, civil society, and the NHRC.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal, Truth and Reconciliation Commission

Detail: One commissioner of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Dr. Madhav Bhattarai, holds a press conference at the commission's office and makes a solo report public.

Conflict victims and civil society members held a demonstration at Maitighar Mandala calling for amendments to the TRC Act. / "Ensure transitional justice. Comply with the Supreme Court order. Establish the commission only after amendment of the Act." — Sit-in demonstration at Maitighar Mandala by civil society and victim families for amendment of the Act and for a victim-friendly commission.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Representative of the International Training Center for Military Personnel (ITCM Panchkhal), Bhumikat Kadel, met with Meena Sunuwar's mother Devi Sunuwar and sister Gita Rasaili (sister of Rina Rasaili) — proposed issues including construction of a memorial (Akshaykosh) in Meena's name. Rejected by the family.

Second meeting: Nepalese Army representatives — Commander of the UN Peacekeeping Mission Nepal Army (Maj. General level) — met with Meena Sunuwar's mother Devi Sunuwar and Gita Rasaili (sister of Rina Rasaili) — proposed issues including construction of a memorial (Akshaykosh) in Meena's name. Rejected by the family.
Parliament obstructed in protest over the killing of Kumar Paudel.
Kumar Paudel, district in-charge of Sarlahi District No. 9 of the CPN (Maoist), taken into custody and killed by police.

Having exhausted domestic remedies, Tikanath Kandel and Ramhari Kandel brought their case to the UN Human Rights Committee through TRIAL International. The Committee found in Kandel v. Nepal that Nepal was responsible for the enforced disappearance of Amrit Kandel, arrested by the Royal Nepal Army in Kathmandu in October 2003 and never seen again, violating his rights to liberty, freedom from torture, and recognition before the law.
Organizations: TRIAL International, Royal Nepal Army, Nepal Army

Detail: The Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs (MOLJPA) develops the ‘Modality for Consultation with Stakeholders before the parliament amends the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Commission on Investigation of Enforced Disappeared Persons’ Act 2014’. The Ministry informs the victims about the Government’s plan to organise consultations in all provinces on the same day.

Collective commitment by leaders including Prachanda and Sher Bahadur Deuba at a ceremony organized by the National Human Rights Commission at Kamala Devi Foundation, Kamaladi — to expedite transitional justice.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: News published in Kantipur regarding a woman who was raped by a dog during the conflict.
Nepal Army's statement: it is not involved and that claims of organized framing of the Nepalese Army are to be investigated. Army's statement: not involved and will cooperate in investigation.

The recommendation committee published a list of candidates for appointments to the TRC and CEIDP, in line with a decision by top political leaders to retain the 2015 commissioners. Conflict victim organizations opposed the list.

Government of Nepal forms a recommendation committee to establish the Commission for Investigation of Disappeared Persons and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Statement of rejection by civil society and the Conflict Victims National Alliance (CVNA).
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Government of Nepal

Detail: On the 13th anniversary of the implementation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, the National Human Rights Commission states it cannot support activities that harm conflict victims' sentiment. Statement.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: On the 13th anniversary of the CPA, Prachanda comes to the victims and pledges to swiftly resolve transitional justice. (news)
NHRC's position made public: transitional justice must be in accordance with the Supreme Court's decision and international standards.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Transitional Justice Reform Process RevivedPolitical parties resume negotiations on amendments to transitional justice legislation.

The Conflict Victim Women National Network (CVWN) was established to address the specific impacts of the conflict on women and to strengthen the participation of conflict-affected women in Nepal’s transitional justice process.

The Conflict Victims Common Platform submitted a memorandum to Foreign Minister Pradeep Kumar Gyawali, calling for meaningful victim participation in amendments to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) Act.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Conflict Victims Common Platform

Detail: The Government invited conflict victims to participate in province-level consultations on proposed amendments to the TRC Act and the Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons (CIEDP) Act.

The Government conducted consultations on transitional justice legislation in all seven provinces. Several victim groups and civil society organizations criticized the process as inadequate and insufficiently inclusive.
At a public event, Pushpa Kamal Dahal ‘Prachanda’ stated that he would take responsibility for “only 5,000” conflict-era deaths, prompting public debate and criticism.
The Recommendation Committee proposed ten commissioners for the TRC and CIEDP despite ongoing demands from victims and civil society to amend the law before making appointments.

The Government appointed new commissioners to the TRC and CIEDP. Victim organizations and civil society groups rejected the appointments, arguing that the commissions lacked a legal framework consistent with Supreme Court rulings and international standards.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, Supreme Court, transitional justice
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Victims and civil society organizations held protests in Kathmandu against the appointment of transitional justice commissioners without prior legal reform.
Advocacy Forum published a briefing paper criticizing the Government’s consultation process on transitional justice legislation as superficial and lacking meaningful victim participation.
The Conflict Victim Women National Network formally announced its establishment.
United Nations human rights experts expressed concern over the state of Nepal’s transitional justice process and urged reforms consistent with international human rights obligations.

Conflict victims and human rights defenders publicly rejected a request from the TRC and CIEDP for cooperation/support, stating they would not engage until the Enforced Disappearance Enquiry, Truth and Reconciliation Commission Act, 2014 was amended in line with the Supreme Court’s 2015 ruling. Conflict Victims Common Platform chair Bhagiram Chaudhari said victims would not support the commissions without an amended law.
Keywords: CVCP, TRC, CIEDP, non-cooperation, Act amendment, Supreme Court 2015, civil society, conflict victims
Organizations: Conflict Victims Common Platform; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP

Detail: Subash Nembang, deputy parliamentary party leader of the Nepal Communist Party and head of a drafting team, said a bill to amend the TRC/CIEDP Act was ready to be tabled in Parliament within about a week, claiming it reflected the Supreme Court ruling, international practice, and victim feedback. CVCP chair Bhagiram Chaudhari said victims had been kept in the dark and would reject a law that failed to secure judicial and reparative justice.
Keywords: TRC Act amendment, Nembang, Parliament, CVCP, transitional justice bill
Organizations: Nepal Communist Party; Conflict Victims Common Platform; Parliament

Detail: The Supreme Court rejected the Government’s attempt to review its landmark 2015 transitional justice ruling, reaffirming that serious human rights violations committed during the conflict cannot be subject to blanket amnesty.

Amnesty International, TRIAL International, the International Commission of Jurists, and Human Rights Watch jointly welcomed the Supreme Court’s late-April rejection of the government’s petition to review its 2015 judgment against amnesties for grave conflict-era crimes, and called for immediate amendment of the 2014 TRC Act in line with that judgment and international obligations.
Keywords: Amnesty International, ICJ, TRIAL International, Human Rights Watch, Supreme Court, amnesty, TRC Act
Organizations: Amnesty International; TRIAL International; International Commission of Jurists; Human Rights Watch

Detail: Conflict victim organizations submitted reports to the United Nations Human Rights Council during Nepal’s Universal Periodic Review, highlighting continued impunity, political interference in transitional justice mechanisms, lack of victim participation, and the failure to investigate conflict-era violations.

On the International Day of the Disappeared, conflict-victim associations (including CVCP, CVSJ, NEFAD) and human rights organisations issued a joint statement calling for an end to delays in justice, fresh consultative amendment of TJ law, and victim-centred commissions. Commemorations in Kathmandu included candlelight vigils and public criticism of politically controlled commissions.
Keywords: International Day of the Disappeared, NEFAD, CVCP, CVSJ, enforced disappearance, transitional justice, candlelight vigil, Kathmandu
Organizations: Conflict Victims’ Common Platform; Conflict Victims’ Society for Justice; NEFAD; ICJ and other co-signatories

Detail: The National Human Rights Commission published a report identifying 286 individuals allegedly responsible for conflict-era human rights violations, including members of state security forces, government officials, and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist).
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: Human Rights Watch and Advocacy Forum published a report documenting 62 cases of alleged extrajudicial killings and highlighting continuing impunity despite court orders for investigations. The report is titled *No Law, No Justice, No State for Victims: The Culture of Impunity in Post-Conflict Nepal* (HRW/Advocacy Forum).
Keywords: killing, No Law No Justice No State for Victims, HRW, Advocacy Forum

Detail: The terms of commissioners appointed to the TRC and CIEDP expired after one year. During their tenure, neither commission completed any investigations into conflict-era violations.

President Bidya Devi Bhandari issued an ordinance amending the TRC/CIEDP law to extend the terms of both commissions and their sitting commissioners by about six months (to mid-July 2021), after their tenure was due to expire on 9 February. Conflict Victims Common Platform chair Maina Karki and other stakeholders publicly opposed another extension without legal reform and performance review, saying the commissions had completed no full investigations.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, ordinance, mandate extension, CVCP, Maina Karki, conflict victims, transitional justice
Organizations: Office of the President; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP; Conflict Victims Common Platform

Detail: Forty-nine national organisations (including CVCP, CVWN, NEFAD, Advocacy Forum, INSEC, Nagarik Aawaz, The Story Kitchen) and eight international organisations (including ICJ, FIDH, AJAR) issued a joint press statement refusing engagement with the TRC and CIEDP if mandates were extended again without amending the TRC Act in line with the Supreme Court’s 2015 ruling. They called for amendment after wide consultations, transparent post-amendment appointments, a public timeline, and asked the UN and other internationals not to engage the commissions until reformed. The Deuba government extended both commissions and office-bearers by a further year on 16 July (already in mastersheet).
Keywords: non-engagement, TRC Act amendment, CVCP, CVWN, NEFAD, ICJ, FIDH, mandate extension, civil society
Organizations: Conflict Victims’ Common Platform; Conflict Victim Women National Network; National Network of Families of Disappeared; Advocacy Forum-Nepal; International Commission of Jurists; FIDH; WOREC (publisher of statement text)

Detail: The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the rape and torture of Devi Maya Nepal, a Tharu indigenous woman raped by six Royal Nepal Army soldiers in Kanchanpur District in August 2002. The decision also recognized the long-term impact of conflict-related sexual violence on children born as a result of rape.

The incoming Sher Bahadur Deuba government extended the terms of the TRC and CIEDP and their office-bearers by a further year. Conflict victims expressed little hope that another extension would deliver investigations, noting repeated prolongations since 2015 with negligible completed cases.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, mandate extension, Deuba government, conflict victims, transitional justice
Organizations: Government of Nepal; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP

Detail: Conflict victim organizations submitted a joint letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, urging reforms to Nepal’s transitional justice laws.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the enforced disappearance of Tej Bahadur Bhandari, arrested in December 2001 and never seen again. The Committee also recognized the suffering experienced by his son, Ram Kumar Bhandari, as a violation of the prohibition against torture and ill-treatment.

On the eve of the 15th anniversary of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, the International Commission of Jurists, and TRIAL International jointly stated that Nepal had made no progress on justice for crimes under international law since 2006; that the TRC and CIEDP had completed no investigations despite tens of thousands of complaints; and that governments had failed to implement the 2015 Supreme Court anti-amnesty ruling. They urged victim-centred reform, a clear consultation/amendment timeline, and international pressure for a credible process.
Keywords: Comprehensive Peace Agreement, 15 years, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, ICJ, TRIAL International, transitional justice, impunity
Organizations: Amnesty International; Human Rights Watch; International Commission of Jurists; TRIAL International

Detail: Victims' Groups Intensify Nationwide AdvocacyConflict victims demand meaningful participation in reform processes and stronger guarantees against impunity.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the torture, rape, and extrajudicial killing of Reena Rasaili (R.R.), a 16-year-old Dalit girl taken from her home by Royal Nepal Army personnel in Kavre District in February 2004. The Committee found violations of her rights to life and freedom from torture.

The UN Human Rights Committee found Nepal responsible for the extrajudicial killing of Anil Chaudhary, a 15-year-old Tharu boy killed by joint security forces while travelling to school in Bardiya District in March 2004.

Newly appointed Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Govinda Sharma Bandi launched a round of government consultations with conflict victims and CSOs to gather input for amending the 2014 TRC/CIEDP Act, framed around truth-seeking, justice, reparation, and institutional reform. The Province 1 session in Biratnagar (~30 victims + organisational reps) was held on 31 May 2022; the ministry said consultations would cover all seven provinces, with a bill targeted for mid-July registration. ICJ later noted seven provincial consultations, one CRSV-focused consultation, and one national consultation preceded the July bill — but that the draft was then presented without letting stakeholders review the text.
Keywords: provincial consultations, Govinda Sharma Bandi, Law Ministry, TRC Act amendment, conflict victims, CRSV consultation
Organizations: Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Conflict Victims’ Common Platform (participants/commentators)

Detail: The mandates of the TRC and CIEDP were extended by three months. By this time, the TRC had registered 63,718 complaints and the CIEDP 3,223 complaints, yet neither commission had completed investigations into conflict-era violations.

The Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs registered in Parliament a “Bill for the Amendment of the Investigation of Enforced Disappeared Persons, Truth and Reconciliation Commission Act, 2071 (2014)” — the first formal parliamentary registration of a TJ amendment bill since the failed 2018 draft. Same day, the government also extended TRC/CIEDP mandates by three months (already a separate mastersheet row). Victims and rights groups soon rejected amnesty/sentencing and definitional flaws (21 Jul demand to withdraw; 31 Jul Maitighar sit-in — already covered). The bill later lapsed when the House term ended ahead of November 2022 elections (September 2022), as noted in OHCHR AL NPL 1/2023.
Keywords: TRC Act amendment bill, Parliament registration, Ministry of Law, 2022 bill, transitional justice, bill lapse
Organizations: Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Parliament of Nepal; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP

Detail: Around seven dozen conflict-victim and human rights organisations demanded that the Ministry of Law and Justice withdraw a bill to amend the TRC/CIEDP Act registered in Parliament, arguing that provisions would enable amnesty for serious conflict-era crimes and ignored victim suggestions from provincial consultations. Conflict Victims Common Platform chair Maina Karki publicly rejected the bill.
Keywords: TRC Act amendment, CIEDP, conflict victims, amnesty, CVCP, civil society, Parliament, Kathmandu
Organizations: Conflict Victims Common Platform; Ministry of Law and Justice

Detail: Conflict victims’ groups including Victims’ Society for Justice, Conflict Victim Women National Network, and Conflict Victims’ Common Platform held a protest/sit-in at Maitighar Mandala, Kathmandu, demanding revision of the Transitional Justice Law Amendment Bill registered on 15 July 2022, objecting especially to provisions they said could grant immunity for serious crimes.
Keywords: Maitighar Mandala, protest, CVWN, CVCP, Victims Society for Justice, TRC bill, survivor advocacy, Kathmandu
Organizations: Victims’ Society for Justice; Conflict Victim Women National Network; Conflict Victims’ Common Platform

Detail: Twenty conflict victims and human rights defenders handed a memorandum addressed to UN Secretary-General António Guterres to UN Resident Coordinator Richard Howard in Kathmandu, seeking the SG’s good offices to press amendment of “perpetrator-friendly” provisions in the bill then before Parliament. Signatories included former NHRC members Gauri Shankar Lal Das and Sushil Pyakurel and former UN ASG Kul Chandra Gautam. The letter criticised murder vs “cruel murder” categorisation, reduced sentencing, due-process gaps, omission of war crimes/crimes against humanity and child soldiers, and the lack of public UN reaction — and was delivered the day the House began deliberations on the bill.
Keywords: UN Secretary-General, memorandum, Richard Howard, TRC amendment bill, conflict victims, child soldiers, amnesty
Organizations: Conflict victim and human rights defenders (ad hoc group); UN Resident Coordinator’s Office Nepal

Detail: The Government of Nepal endorsed the Second National Action Plan (NAP II) on UN Security Council Resolutions 1325 and 1820 (FY 2022/23–2024/25), with a specific focus on conflict-related sexual violence survivors — including recognition as conflict victims, access to services, justice, and livelihood support — building on NAP I (2011).
Keywords: NAP II, Women Peace and Security, UNSCR 1325, UNSCR 1820, CRSV, conflict-related sexual violence, Ministry of Home Affairs
Organizations: Government of Nepal; Ministry of Home Affairs; UN Women

Detail: With commissioner terms expiring, the government extended the institutional terms of the TRC and CIEDP without appointing chairs or members, leaving the transitional justice bodies without sitting commissioners and stalling case work.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, vacant commissioners, mandate extension, transitional justice, institutional stall
Organizations: Government of Nepal; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP

Detail: Political Consensus on Reform Begins to EmergeMajor political actors move closer to agreement on unresolved transitional justice provisions.

The Aparajita Foundation was established by Devi Khadka, a survivor of conflict-era sexual violence, to support women survivors. The survivor-led organization expanded to more than 800 members, providing counseling, health services, documentation of conflict-era sexual violence cases, and advocacy for amendments to the TRC Act.
Devi Sunuwar, mother of Maina Sunuwar, filed an additional writ petition seeking accountability for her daughter's killing.
The Supreme Court consolidated all three related cases and scheduled a verdict.

A CSO coalition titled Victim and Civil Society for Women, Peace and Security was formed in 2023 with about 15 member organisations, led by the Conflict Victim Women National Network (CVWN), to coordinate advocacy for implementation of Nepal’s NAP II on Women, Peace and Security and inclusion of conflict-victim women in related decision-making.
Keywords: CVWN, Women Peace and Security, NAP II, civil society coalition, survivor women, advocacy
Organizations: Conflict Victim Women National Network; Victim and Civil Society for Women, Peace and Security (coalition)

Detail: Advocacy Forum-Nepal, Conflict Victims Women's Network, Human Rights and Justice Center, Nagarik Aawaz, and The Story Kitchen issued a joint statement on International Women’s Day calling for amendments to the TRC Act, implementation of National Action Plan II, and meaningful participation of conflict-affected women in transitional justice processes.
Organizations: Advocacy Forum-Nepal, Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Nagarik Aawaz

Detail: A bill to amend the TRC Act was tabled in Parliament. The bill included some victim demands, including provisions on reparations and interim relief, but excluded several serious violations from the definition of grave human rights violations, raising concerns about potential amnesty.
Conflict victim groups issued a joint statement opposing provisions in the proposed TRC amendment that could allow amnesty for serious conflict-era crimes.

Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the International Commission of Jurists criticized the proposed TRC amendment bill, stating that it conflicted with Supreme Court rulings and international human rights standards and lacked meaningful victim consultation.
Organizations: Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, International Commission of Jurists, Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Four UN Special Procedures mandate-holders — Special Rapporteur on truth, justice, reparation and guarantees of non-recurrence (Fabian Salvioli); Chair-Rapporteur of the WGEID (Aua Baldé); Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions (Morris Tidball-Binz); and Special Rapporteur on violence against women and girls (Reem Alsalem) — sent allegation letter AL NPL 1/2023 to Nepal concerning the amendment bill submitted to Parliament on 19 March 2023. While noting positive reparation and gender/disability language, they warned that the bill’s two-tier violation categories, amnesty reach, sentence mitigation, statute-of-limitations silence, and consultation gaps appeared inconsistent with ICCPR obligations and the 2015 Supreme Court ruling, and offered technical assistance.
Keywords: UN Special Procedures, AL NPL 1/2023, Fabian Salvioli, WGEID, TRC amendment bill, amnesty, international standards
Organizations: UN Special Rapporteur on truth, justice, reparation and non-recurrence; Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances; OHCHR Special Procedures

Detail: Nepal’s Supreme Court directed the government to include conflict-era torture and sexual-violence survivors in the interim relief programme, finding discriminatory exclusion of those categories from relief procedures. The bench (Justices Sapana Pradhan Malla and Hari Prasad Phuyal) also addressed related relief barriers for remarried widows of conflict victims.
Keywords: Supreme Court, interim relief, sexual violence, torture, conflict victims, reparations, Sapana Pradhan Malla
Organizations: Supreme Court of Nepal; Government of Nepal

Detail: After failing to pass the TRC Act amendment, the Cabinet used Section 42 (“removal of difficulties”) to extend the institutional terms of the TRC and CIEDP by six months to 14 January 2024 (terms had been due to expire around mid-July 2023). The commissions had remained without chairs/members since mid-2022, so the extension kept the bodies legally alive but operationally defunct pending law reform and new appointments. The decision was required to be presented to Parliament within 30 days.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, mandate extension, Section 42, vacant commissioners, Cabinet, transitional justice
Organizations: Government of Nepal; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP

Detail: The Cabinet extended the institutional terms of the still-vacant TRC and CIEDP to mid-July 2024 via Section 42 (“removal of difficulties”), continuing the pattern of keeping the commissions legally alive without chairs or members pending amendment of the TRC Act and new appointments.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, mandate extension, Section 42, vacant commissioners, Cabinet, transitional justice
Organizations: Government of Nepal; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP

Detail: Human Rights Watch published the report “Breaking Barriers to Justice: Nepal’s Long Struggle for Accountability, Truth and Reparations,” documenting stalled transitional justice, vacant TRC/CIEDP leadership after October 2022, and the continued absence of completed conflict-era investigations despite tens of thousands of registered complaints.
Keywords: Human Rights Watch, transitional justice, accountability, TRC, CIEDP, civil society documentation, report

Detail: Ram Bhandari, a conflict victim leader whose father was forcibly disappeared in 2001, addressed the UN Security Council in New York on behalf of the Global Alliance of the Missing, advocating for truth, legal protections for missing persons, and victim participation in peace processes.
A three-member cross-party panel comprising Ramesh Lekhak, Mahesh Bartaula, and Janardan Sharma was formed to negotiate provisions of the bill to amend the TRC Act.

Transitional Justice Act AmendedParliament adopts long-awaited amendments to the transitional justice framework after years of debate. While some longstanding legal obstacles are addressed, victims, civil society organizations, and experts continue to debate whether the law fully meets expectations regarding truth, accountability, and victims' rights.

Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the International Commission of Jurists issued a joint assessment that Nepal’s amended transitional justice law (passed by the lower house on 14 August 2024) included positive accountability and reparation elements but retained flaws — including a possible 75% sentence reduction for serious violations (excluding rape/serious sexual violence) — that could undermine justice.
Keywords: TRC Act, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, ICJ, sentence reduction, amnesty concern, civil society, 2024
Organizations: Amnesty International; Human Rights Watch; International Commission of Jurists

Detail: Parliament passed the amended TRC Act despite protests by conflict victims and human rights advocates. The law classified intentional and arbitrary killings as serious human rights violations but retained provisions allowing substantial sentence reductions for most serious violations. Victims and survivors were not consulted during final negotiations. Legislative sequence: House of Representatives endorsed the Third Amendment on 14 August 2024; the National Assembly passed it on 22 August; the Speaker certified/forwarded it on 28 August; and the President authenticated it on 29 August 2024 (separate authentication row).
