Keywords: TRC, killing, transitional justice, protest, House of Representatives, National Assembly, Third Amendment, Speaker certification

Detail: The Supreme Court postponed its verdict in the Maina Sunuwar case without setting a new date. Maina Sunuwar, a 15-year-old girl killed by Nepal Army personnel in 2004, remained without justice as three officers convicted in 2017 had not been arrested or served their sentences.
Organizations: Nepal Army, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: Advocacy Forum-Nepal, with Nagarik Aawaz and the Conflict Victims Women’s National Network (CVWN), organised a strategic meeting in Kathmandu on consolidating conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV) data ahead of TRC work, discussing informed consent, data-sharing standards, and coordination among survivor organisations including engagement challenges with survivor-leader Devi Khadka / Aprajit networks.
Keywords: CRSV, sexual violence data, Advocacy Forum, Nagarik Aawaz, CVWN, survivor organising, TRC, Kathmandu
Organizations: Advocacy Forum-Nepal; Nagarik Aawaz; Conflict Victims Women’s National Network

Detail: President Ram Chandra Paudel authenticated the Enforced Disappearances Enquiry, Truth and Reconciliation Commission Act (Third Amendment) Bill, 2024 under Article 113(2) of the Constitution, after the House of Representatives endorsed it on 14 August, the National Assembly on 22 August, and the Speaker certified/forwarded it on 28 August. Authentication completed the legislative process begun with the March 2023 bill and the July 2024 three-party panel, legally enabling reconstitution of the long-vacant TRC and CIEDP (commissioner nomination efforts followed in Oct–Dec 2024 — already in mastersheet).
Keywords: President authentication, Ram Chandra Paudel, TRC Act Third Amendment, House of Representatives, National Assembly, Article 113
Organizations: Office of the President; Parliament of Nepal; Truth and Reconciliation Commission; CIEDP

Detail: The government established a five-member recommendation committee led by former Chief Justice Om Prakash Mishra to nominate commissioners for the TRC and the Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons (CIEDP), which had been inactive since July 2022.
The recommendation committee led by Om Prakash Mishra completed its tenure without selecting commissioners for the TRC and CIEDP after failing to reach consensus.

Transitional Justice Leadership Selection Sparks Public DebateVictims' groups, civil society organizations, and human rights defenders call for a transparent, independent, and victim-centered process for appointing commissioners to the TRC and CIEDP. Concerns are raised regarding transparency, consultation, independence, and political influence in the selection process. Several shortlisted candidates withdraw their candidacies amid concerns regarding transparency, independence, and public confidence in the selection process.

New TRC and CIEDP Commissioners AppointedThe Government appoints new commissioners to the TRC and CIEDP, seeking to revive long-stalled investigations into conflict-era violations, enforced disappearances, truth-seeking, reparations, and accountability.
Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli appointed former Law Minister Agni Kharel as Transitional Justice Advisor to facilitate political consensus on advancing the transitional justice process.

Leaders of the three major political parties agreed to form a new recommendation committee for the TRC and CIEDP. Former Chief Justice Om Prakash Mishra, former Attorney General Kham Bahadur Khati, Arjun Karki, Stella Tamang, and Lily Thapa were appointed as members.

Twelve organizations from the Gender and Transitional Justice Network, including the Conflict Victim Women National Network, submitted recommendations to the Ministry of Law calling for a gender-responsive transitional justice process and improved protections for survivors of conflict-related sexual violence.
Thirty-six victim organizations and activists rejected the shortlisted candidates and demanded the formation of a new independent recommendation committee.
Representatives of 39 victim groups met Pushpa Kamal Dahal and separately met Sher Bahadur Deuba, urging support for a victim-centered, transparent, and credible transitional justice process.
Ten Nepali human rights organizations expressed solidarity with victims’ concerns regarding the commission selection process and urged the government to address their demands.
Conflict victims organized a protest against what they described as a politically influenced and non-transparent commission appointment process.

The recommendation committee submitted its final list of candidates for the TRC and CIEDP despite ongoing objections from victim groups. Victims and survivors staged a sit-in protest at the National Human Rights Commission in Lalitpur.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, Lalitpur, transitional justice, protest
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal, Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP

Detail: Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the International Commission of Jurists publicly supported victims’ demands for a credible and transparent appointment process.
Organizations: Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, International Commission of Jurists

Detail: Conflict victim families from 12 districts in Lumbini Province gathered in Nepalgunj to oppose the unilateral appointment of commissioners to the TRC and CIEDP.

Representatives of 39 victim and survivor groups met diplomats from more than 19 countries and the UN Resident Coordinator to express concerns about the transitional justice process. The same day, they submitted an open letter to the Prime Minister demanding a transparent appointment process. Later that evening, the government appointed commissioners to the TRC and CIEDP for four-year terms.

The Conflict Victim Women Network, Conflict Victims Common Platform, and the National Network of Families of the Disappeared and Missing Nepal rejected the appointments and urged appointees to decline their positions in solidarity with victims.
Conflict victims submitted a petition requesting information about the commissioner selection process under Nepal’s Right to Information framework.
The government formally constituted the TRC and CIEDP. Liladevi Gadtoula was sworn in as Chairperson of the CIEDP and Mahesh Thapa as Chairperson of the TRC.

The TRC opened a three-month complaint registration period for survivors of conflict-related sexual violence. Survivor groups noted that many cases remained undocumented and expressed concerns about the process.
The Gender and Transitional Justice Network and survivor organizations criticized the TRC complaint process, citing concerns over victim consultation, privacy, security, mental health, and dignity.
Victim representatives met President Ramchandra Paudel, urging intervention in the transitional justice process. Paudel expressed support for their concerns.

The Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court ordered the reopening of the criminal investigation into Agni Sapkota, former Speaker of the House of Representatives and senior leader of the CPN (Maoist Centre), in connection with a conflict-era killing.

The Missing Warrior Family Society Nepal and the Bipin Bhandari Foundation organized a memorial conference in Kathmandu for families of the disappeared, calling for public acknowledgment, victim participation, and independent truth-seeking mechanisms.
Women survivors of conflict-related sexual violence held a candlelight vigil in Kathmandu, publicly demanding truth, recognition, and justice.
Government representatives, political party leaders, and conflict victim representatives held dialogue aimed at rebuilding trust and addressing concerns regarding the transitional justice process.
Conflict victim representatives submitted an urgent appeal to UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk, seeking international support for their demands.
Thakurbaba Municipality in Bardiya District introduced a local reparations program providing monthly allowances to wives of disappeared persons, addressing a gap in national support measures.

The Center for Human Rights and Victims of Violations at Kathmandu University launched The Survivor’s Record, a victim-led newsletter on transitional justice and victim movements, led by Dr. Ram Bhandari.

Forty-seven victim groups and 26 civil society organizations submitted a report to the UN Human Rights Council highlighting concerns about legal shortcomings, political interference, and commission appointments.

During a parliamentary session, victim leader and Member of Parliament Maina Karki questioned the government's commitment to transitional justice. Prime Minister Oli reaffirmed support for dialogue with victims and recognition of conflict-affected communities.
Victim representatives met senior government officials and political representatives at the Prime Minister’s Office to discuss transitional justice concerns.

More than a dozen victim and survivor representatives attempted to file a writ petition signed by 334 individuals from 67 districts challenging provisions of the TRC Act and the legitimacy of the commissions. The petition was not immediately registered.
Victim representatives returned to the Supreme Court seeking registration of the writ petition and were informed that further consultation was required.
The registrar formally rejected the writ petition. Victim representatives appealed the decision.
Brihat Nagarik Aandolan organized a public discussion on victim opposition to the transitional justice commissions, featuring victim leaders and legal experts.
The Supreme Court overturned the registrar’s decision and ordered the petition to be registered.
Victim groups organized a discussion in Kathmandu advocating for victim-centered alternatives to state-appointed transitional justice commissions.

On the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances, victims, civil society groups, and community members held candlelight vigils across Nepal to remember the disappeared and call for justice. Commemorative events took place in more than 30 districts.

The TRC reported receiving 15,191 new complaints, including 3,912 related to rape or sexual violence. Survivors of conflict-related sexual violence submitted more than 90 percent of these complaints directly. Devi Khadka, a survivor and activist, submitted 200 complaints collected from survivors, many of whom requested confidentiality protections.
Security forces used live ammunition, tear gas, water cannons, and rubber bullets against Gen-Z-led protests against corruption, economic inequality, and government policies.
At least 19 civilian protesters were killed and hundreds injured. Human rights organizations condemned the use of excessive force and arbitrary arrests.

Following escalating unrest, destruction of public property, and political instability, several cabinet ministers and Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli resigned. The military assumed responsibility for maintaining public order.

Following negotiations involving youth leaders, the Nepal Army, and President Ramchandra Paudel, former Chief Justice Sushila Karki was appointed Interim Prime Minister. The reported death toll from the unrest rose to 72 people, including 59 protesters killed by security forces.

On the 11th anniversary of Nanda Prasad Adhikari’s death, human rights defenders and victim leaders visited Ganga Maya Adhikari and renewed calls for accountability for the killing of their son, Krishna Prasad Adhikari.

Devi Khadka, a survivor of conflict-related sexual violence and women’s rights activist, addressed the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on strengthening gender perspectives in transitional justice processes.
Conflict victim representatives met senior advisors to the Interim Prime Minister to raise concerns about the incomplete transitional justice process.
Conflict victim organizations issued a statement marking 19 years since the Comprehensive Peace Accord and reiterating concerns about the lack of progress in transitional justice.

On the 19th anniversary of the Comprehensive Peace Accord, conflict victims organized protests across all seven provinces demanding the resignation of current commissioners and a transparent, independent, and victim-centered transitional justice process.

Nepali civil society representatives raised concerns about transitional justice during a Universal Periodic Review pre-session in Geneva, highlighting dissatisfaction with the appointment of TRC and CIEDP commissioners.

The National Network of Disabled Conflict Victims marked the International Day of Persons with Disabilities through a forum theatre performance and an exhibition highlighting the experiences of conflict-affected persons with disabilities.

The National Network of Disabled Conflict Victims released a study reporting that many civilians who acquired disabilities during the armed conflict had received insufficient or no compensation from the state.
The Nepal Human Rights International Film Festival screened Devi, a documentary about Devi Khadka, a survivor of conflict-related sexual violence and advocate for justice for survivors.

Victim and survivor groups published a position paper rejecting the existing TRC and CIEDP commissions as politically controlled and lacking victim participation. They called for the resignation or suspension of commissioners and a new transparent, merit-based appointment process.

The Supreme Court's Judgement Execution Unit directed the government and parliament to implement the Court's ruling on conflict victims' right to social justice, ordering continued support for conflict victims, martyrs' families, and historically marginalized communities in education, health, employment, housing, and social security.

Conflict victims staged a sit-in protest outside the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs in Kathmandu, opposing consultations on transitional justice regulations and demanding a new victim-centered process.
Victim leaders met Home Minister Om Prakash Aryal, reiterating their rejection of the current TRC and CIEDP and calling for meaningful victim participation in any future process.
The Center for Human Rights and Victims of Violations and Amnesty International Nepal organized a public discussion in Kathmandu on the prospects of a victim-centered civil commission.

During Nepal's Universal Periodic Review in Geneva, the government highlighted the reconstitution of the TRC and CIEDP as progress in transitional justice. Victim groups and international actors raised concerns regarding political appointments, independence, and victim participation.

The Human Rights and Justice Centre and the Center for Human Rights and Victims of Violations launched Saturday Sambad, a dialogue initiative focused on transitional justice, human rights, and democratization.
Victim leaders issued a joint appeal urging political parties contesting the upcoming election to commit to human rights, victim-centered transitional justice, and measures to end impunity.

As parties finalized candidates for the general election, several conflict survivors and individuals accused or implicated in conflict-era violations contested parliamentary seats, prompting concern among victim groups regarding accountability.

The Supreme Court scheduled a final hearing in a petition filed by Lenin Bista, a former Maoist child soldier, challenging the exclusion of child recruitment from the category of serious human rights violations and seeking reparations for former child soldiers.
The family of Maina Sunuwar, a 15-year-old student abducted, tortured, and killed by Royal Nepal Army personnel in 2004, organized a memorial event at her former school in Kavre.
Several individuals facing unresolved conflict-era human rights allegations or convictions were elected to parliament, raising concerns among victims and survivors about continuing impunity.

On the International Day for the Right to Truth, victim groups organized a public discussion in Kathmandu calling for the removal of current commissioners and the establishment of a credible, victim-centered transitional justice process.
Victim groups and civil society organizations submitted a letter to the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights calling for truth, justice, and accountability for conflict-era violations in Nepal.

The Supreme Court ordered the prompt resolution of conflict-era cases and struck down amnesty provisions in the TRC Act that could allow pardons or sentence reductions for perpetrators of serious human rights violations.
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: The National Network of Conflict-Affected Persons with Disabilities published Living Memories of War – Part Two, documenting the experiences of persons who acquired disabilities during the armed conflict.
Community members commemorated Arjun Chaudhary (21), Indra Bahadur Chaudhary (18), and Bijay Chaudhary (14), three Tharu civilians tortured and killed by security forces in Dang District in 2004.

Forty conflict victim organizations sent an open letter to Prime Minister Shah, demanding amendments to the TRC Act, dismissal of current commissioners, a transparent appointment process, and meaningful victim participation.
The family of Purna Poudel, a student leader forcibly disappeared in 2002, organized a memorial event in Pokhara. His mother Motimaya Poudel, aged 85, renewed calls for truth regarding his fate.

Victim and survivor groups appealed to UN Special Rapporteur Bernard Duhaime to support victim-centered transitional justice and highlighted concerns regarding commission appointments, exclusion of victims, handling of conflict-related sexual violence, and unmet socio-economic needs.

Victims and survivors honored Kalyan Budhathoki (63), a conflict victim leader and co-founder of the Conflict Victim Common Platform, following his death on 8 April 2026 after more than two decades of advocacy.

The Government of Nepal postponed the planned visit of UN Special Rapporteur Bernard Duhaime for a second time. Victim groups expressed disappointment, having prepared to present concerns regarding transitional justice.

The Supreme Court ordered the government, TRC, and CIEDP to address all pending submissions from victims and survivors and ruled that prolonged delays in responding to complaints violate victims' rights.
Keywords: TRC, CIEDP, Supreme Court, transitional justice
Organizations: Truth and Reconciliation Commission, CIEDP, Supreme Court of Nepal

Detail: A presidential ordinance terminated public appointments made before 26 March 2026, resulting in the removal of more than 1,500 officials across multiple sectors.
The National Human Rights Commission urged the government to prioritize completion of the transitional justice process among its key human rights commitments.
Organizations: National Human Rights Commission of Nepal

Detail: President Ramchandra Paudel presented the Government Policy and Programme to Parliament, including a commitment to concluding Nepal's transitional justice process.

More than 100 families of disappeared persons gathered in Kathmandu to commemorate their relatives and called for national recognition of the disappeared, memorialization initiatives, and inclusion of conflict history in education.
